**These tabular models place their modeling effort in different places.** TabNet selects feature subsets through sequential attention masks. FT-Transformer embeds columns as tokens and learns interactions with self-attention. TabPFN uses pretraining across tasks so labeled rows can condition predictions in context. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.07442) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11959) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01848)

TabNet and FT-Transformer typically optimize weights on the target dataset. TabPFN amortizes much of that work into pretraining, making its task prior important. Attention masks can aid inspection but should not be treated as causal explanations.

**Trees remain a necessary baseline.** Compare against tuned GBDTs using the same features, split, and tuning budget. Include categorical handling, missing data, calibration, and resource constraints. A neural result with extensive tuning is not fairly compared with an untouched default tree model.

Dataset size, feature semantics, and shift determine suitability. Check actual implementation limits rather than assuming every version supports the same rows, classes, and columns. No architecture wins on every table. Choose on measured generalization and operational cost, not the novelty of the model family.

**Technical details and references.**

TabNet uses sequential attentive feature masks to focus each decision step on selected columns; the masks aid inspection but are not causal explanations. FT-Transformer maps numerical/categorical features into tokens and applies self-attention, providing a strong supervised tabular neural baseline. TabPFN learns a prior over tasks during pretraining and conditions on labeled rows to predict new rows in context. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.07442) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11959) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01848)

Compare them with tuned GBDTs on leakage-free splits, including categorical handling, missingness, row/feature limits, compute, and calibration. TabPFN shifts much optimization cost to pretraining, while TabNet/FT-Transformer typically optimize on the target dataset. No method wins on every table; dataset size, feature semantics, distribution shift, and pretrained assumptions determine suitability. Match evaluation budgets rather than comparing tuned neural models to default tree settings.
